A NEGRO LYNCHED.
GUTHRIE, Ky., August 27.—On Tuesday morning a colored man named Green Ellis assaulted Mrs. Duncan, two miles north of here, with intent to commit robbery. After beating her severely and taking $12 that was on her person, he left her for dead. She recovered sufficiently to get home and report the facts. Ellis was caught here yesterday and had his trial, and was to have been sent to the County Jail to-day. Last night, about 10 o'clock, between twenty-five and fifty men rode into town, overpowered the guard, and removed Ellis. He was hanged not far from the town.

THE GALLOWS CHEATED.

PALESTINE, Tex., Aug. 27.—Great excitement has been caused here by the announcement that Roland Rucker, whom was to have been hanged here to-day for the murder of R. P. Grayson and wife, when the prison authorities visited the cell at 5 o'clock, this morning, found the man in the last agonies of death. Near him was a large pool of blood and blood was issuing from a wound in his left wrist which he had made with his penknife. On examination they found the arteries had been severed. How Rucker got possession of the knife is a mystery.

TIRED OF LIFE.

New York, Aug. 27.—A dispatch from Paris states, that Miss Candace Molney, once a well known milliner here, and who was a witness in the celebrated Newell divorce suit in April last, had killed herself at the Hotel de France, at Pan. In a letter written before her death she says: "I am weary of life and want rest," and asks to be placed in a coffin in the dress she wore when she died.

JUSTIFIABLE HOMICIDE.

ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 27.—Night before last, near Cochran, four young white men, disguised, went to a negro cabin, broke down the door, and fired into the cabin. The occupant, John Brown, seized his gun, fired both barrels and killed two brothers named Dykes. The tops of their heads were blown off. The negro made his escape. The coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide.

FRAUDULENT EMIGRANT RAILROAD TICKETS.

New York, Aug. 27.—It is reported here that a large number of forged passage tickets over railroad lines west, have been put out, and that the police are watching the movements of parties suspected of being concerned in the fraudulent issue.

ARMY QUARTERS DESTROYED.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 27.—Gen. McDowell telegraphs the following received from Fort Mojave, Arizona, and dated the 22d. During a furious storm the company quarters were blown down and three men killed and several others wounded. The officers' quarters were destroyed, and the hospital and store house much damaged. The strom is still raging.

EXECUTIONS IN TEXAS.

Waco, Texas, Aug. 27.—Lynchfield Burks was hanged here at 2 o'clock this afternoon for assaulting a girl 9 years old, named Sarah McBee. He died denying his guilt.

DALLAS, Texas, Aug. 27.—This afternoon Allen Wright was hung for the murder of Jessie Wycks. Both were colored men. Nearly 3000 people gathered around the scaffold, women predominating. Some cow-boys came hundreds of miles to see the execution. The condemned man was to have been executed last Friday, but Gov. Roberts, in answer to a numerously signed petition, granted him a respite until to-day, in order to better prepare for death.

ESCAPED FROM JAIL. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. KANSAS CITY, Mo., Aug. 27.—Thomas Blake, a burglar, who for some time has been waiting a ten years' sentence, made a most ingenious escape from the County Jail here to-day. He occupied a cell with one Jenkins, sentenced to ten days in jail for larceny, and when the officers came this afternoon to release Jenkins, Blake passed out, attired in his cell-mate's clothes, and escaped, the change not being discovered until 0 o'clock. Blake is a professional burglar, and persuaded Jenkins to change places, stating the law could not harm him, and that the officers would have to release him at once. The men were almost exact counterparts, which made the game easier to carry out. HUNG BY A MOR.

A KENTUCKY LYNCHING.

Louisville, Ky., Aug. 27.—A Bowling Green Courier-Journal special says: "Information has just reached here of the lynching of a negro man named Green Ellis, near Guthrie, Ky., last night. Mrs. Duncan, who lives three miles from Guthrie, went to town Tuesday with a lot of chickens and vegetables. As she was returning home after having disposed of her barter, Ellis met her in the road and knocked her from her horse. After she fell he struck her several times more. As she fell she managed to get out a small pocket-knife, and made every exertion to defend herself, inflicting several cuts upon her assailant. She, however, by repeated blows, was rendered insensible. The pocketbook, containing $12, was taken from her, and her body dragged twenty-five or thirty yards from the road and placed behind a large log. Her family commenced search for her, and when found, near dark, in the condition above stated, she told her story, identified Ellis as the party who attacked her, and described a flesh wound she made upon him. Ellis was arrested, carried to Guthrie, and placed in the caboose. Intense excitement and indignation at the outrage was manifested everywhere, and although some citizens counseled moderation and advised their friends and relatives to let the law avenge the crime, it was all to no purpose. A body of men, one hundred and over in number, quietly rode to Guthrie between midnight and day this morning and forebly got possession of the accused, carried him back some three miles distant to the scene of the crime, and swung him from a tree only a few feet from where he struck the first blow. This is the second affair of a most horrible nature that has occurred in this county within the past year."

West Toronto Election—The International Bridge in Court—Grain-Shipments from Montreal to Great Britain.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

MONTREAL, Aug. 27.—Laborers on Sec. 11 of the Lachine Canal to the number of 450 struck work to-day for an advance of wages. They demand $1.25 instead of $4, which they have been receiving. Sixty men who were at work on the section declined to join the strikers. One of these, named Michael Walsh, was attacked by the disaffected us he was proceeding to the works after dinner and beaten severely. The strikers are mostly French Canadians, who will go logging if they do not obtain the advance of 25 cents per day. Further violence is apprehended.

The McNamee robbery case was in court to-day again on a caplus case, when Jones and Trainor, the accused, were examined with a view to show that they had acknowledged taking the money and agreed to compromise with McNamee by returning $9,000 of the $15,000 if he would let them off from prosecuting. They denied any such agreement. They have placed a seizure on the $5,000 which the defective found in their possession.

The receipts of grain at this port this season to date were 1,539,078 bushels, an excess over the same period last year.

A swindler named Dunning C. Briggs, from Lewiston, Me., after defrauding his creditors out of $22,000, came to this city to escape prosecution. He was followed by a Boston detective, who wormed himself into Briggs' confidence, and under an adroit plan investigated the Lewiston man into American territory under the plea of carrying on a smuggling business, and then had him arrested.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

QRTAWA, Aug. 27.—Quartermaster Pocklington and Sergi, Edgar, of the Northwest Mounted Police, are in the city. The former was stationed at Fort McLeod, and the latter at Fort Saskatchewan. They left Fort McLeod on the 21st of July last, and came via the Powers' line of steamers down the Missouri, taking the boat at Wolf Point, which place they reached on the 6th of August. It was reported there that Sitting Bull had passed through with forty lodges on route for the buffalo hunting-grounds. Ten miles below, at Poplar Creek, are located 3,000 lodges of Sioux, whose actions so alarmed the United States Indian Agent, Maj. Porter, that he sent his wife and family to Bismarck for safety. The travelers also learned that the Indians intended to hold a sun-dance, which is a great festival for them, and rigidly observed. After the dance a council is to be held, and then will be decided which course or policy is to be pursued until the following year. Before Messrs. Pocklington and Edgar left Fort McLeod the annual payments had been made to the Indians. Payments commenced on the 26th of July, the following tribes being paid: The Bloods, Blackfeet, Plegans, and the Stonys. The Chiefs received $25, the Deputy Chiefs $15, the men, women, and children $5 each.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Tononto, Aug. 27.—The election for West Toronto, to fill the vacancy in the Dominion Parliament caused by the appointment of the Hon. J. B. Robinson to the Lieutenant-Governorship of Ontario, takes place tomorrow. For the past week political meetings have been held nightly in the constituency, and the campaign has been prosecuted with vigor on all sides. The candidates are Thomas Ryan, Reformer; James Beatty, Jr., Conservative; A. W. Wright, Paper-Money advocate; and F. C. Capreol, Independent, and an advocate of the Georgian-Bay Canal scheme. Mr. Wright does not expect to be elected, but takes this opportunity to get the Rug-Baby issue before the people. Mr. Capreol's chances are hopeless. 'The Georgian-Bay enterprise is one that will take a long time to induce capitalists on either side of the water to take hold of it; and yet the Georgian-Bay enterprise is a more feasible one than the Canada Pacific Railway, and would be of greater service to the country if it were pusl0 to completion. The contest is virtually between Mr. Ryan and Mr. Bentty. Mr. Ryan is a pronounced Free-Trader, and Mr. Bentty a Protectionist and supporter of the Government. The National Policy is, therefore, on trial, and the issue is watched for with considerable interest.

A corporation was created by the Legislature of the State of New York, in 1857, for the construction of a bridge across the Niagara River, from the City of Buffalo to some point near Fort Erie, for the passage of teams, carriages, and railway trains. A few months later, the Parliament of Canada created a corporation for a similar purpose, with power to unite with any company chartered by the people of the State of New York. Under these statutes the International Bridge was constructed. The Bridge Company claims that it has power under its charter to impose tolls for the use of its bridge, and has imposed tolls on the various railways making use of it. A large amount of money (over $100,000) being due for tolls from the Canada Southern Railway, a bill was filed in the Court of Chancery for the purpose of compelling the railway to pay the same. The defense was, that the tolls were excessive; that the Bridge Company had no power to impose them; that the Grand Trunk Railway is the lessee of the bridge, and that the charges were made wholly in the interest of that company.

A Colored Man Lynched.

BOWLING GREEN, Ky., August 28.—Green Ellis, a colored man, was lynched near Guthrie, Ky., night before last. Mrs. Duncan, who lives three miles from Guthrie, went to town on Tuesday with chickens and vegetables, while returning home after having disposed of her barter, Ellis met her on the road and knocked her from her horse. After she fell he struck her several times more. As she fell she drew a small pocket knife and inflicted several cuts upon her assailant. She, however, by repeated blows, was rendered insensible. Her pocket-book, containing $12, was taken from her. Her body was dragged twenty-five or thirty yards from the road and placed behind a huge log. Her family commenced a search for her, and when found at dark was in the condition above stated. She told her story and identified Ellis as the party who attacked her, and described the flesh wounds she made upon him. Ellis was arrested, carried to Guthrie and placed in the calaboose. Intense excitement and indignation at the outrage were manifested everywhere, and although some citizens and relatives counseled moderation, and advised to let the law avenge the crime, a body of men, over 100 in number, quietly rode to Guthrie between midnight and daylight yesterday morning, forcibly seized the accused, carried him back some three miles distant to the scene of the crime, and swung him from a tree only a few feet from where he struck the first blow. This is the second affair of this nature that has occurred in this county in the last year. Mrs. Duncan is highly respected. The criminal was an idle and worthless negro.

Grant at Galena.

Galena, August 28.—Last night Hon. Philo A. Orton, in a speech to a Republican mass meeting, gave his reasons for leaving the Democratic party, with which he has acted for twenty years. He introduced Gen. Grant, who said: I did not intend to speak when I came here to-night. I am very much like Judge Orton. I have never made a Republican speech in my life, or any kind of a political speech. I am sure it would require some time and much preparation to make one of any length. I can, of course, go a little further than Judge Orton, and say that I never voted a Republican Presidential ticket in my life, and but one Democratic ticket, and that was many years ago, when I was a young man; but I will pledge you my word, here to-night, that if I am spared, although I shall be at some distance from you on the 2d of November, I shall return to Galena to cast one Republican vote for President of the United States, and I hope the city of Galena will cast a round Republican vote, such as it has never cast before.

A Colored Virginia Democrat Abroad.
SPEECH IN WILMINGTON, DEL., TUESDAY— SOUTHERN OUTRAGES DISCUSSED—HOOTED AND JEERED AND PURSUED TO THE TRAIN BY A CROWD OF BLACKS AND WHITES.
[Wilmington Every Evening.]
H. Harris, the colored.
[Wilmington Every Evening.]

John H. Harris, the colored Democrat hailing from Virginia, spoke to a mixed crowd at the City Hall Tuesday evening.

He showed how Republican tricksters in the South made colored men their tools, and when they met with injury the rush was made to the telegraph office and a new outrage was born. He spoke of the threats made against him in case he should speak, and said he had been told that there was a party of 300 in town who proposed to mob him in case he took the platform. "Ain't that nice?" said he, and the crowd jeered.

He then touched on other threats and returned to an arraignment of the Republican party in several particulars, and closed the whole speech with an appeal for help financially, getting a little hard money. His speech, while it contained a number of truths, was a rambling, disconnected affair. It lasted for about an hour. At the close he proposed three cheers for Hancock and English, but received no response. As the crowd turned to go out some one proposed three cheers for Garfield, which were given, but were nearly drowned at the close by the succeeding hoots. Bailiff Daley turned out the lights, and thus the meeting ended.

During the speech such remarks were made as "We'll put you in the harness;" "We'll bridle you," &c., and loud laughing was frequently indulged in.

ON THE OUTSIDE,

while the meeting was in progress, a party of white men, among whom were some members of the Young Men's Republican Club, had an animated conversation about the speaker, some of them saying he ought to be rotten-egged, and being seemingly inclined to do it. When Harris came out of the hall he was immediately surrounded, so that he was almost unable to make any progress. He took a drink of water at the fountain, and then went up toward Sixth street, but was followed so closely that he turned into Captain Shaw's restaurant, where he remained for about ten minutes.

THE MARCH DOWN TOWN.

At the end of that time he came out of the restaurant and started down town, but had not gotten half a square before he was surrounded again. Being on Market street, the crowd was not very noisy, but hugged the long orator close. He proceeded down to Fourth street, where Ned Leary, who did not want to see him hurt, did him a good turn by taking him into the Swan Hotel. The crowd then stopped for a moment, not penetrating the plan, while Harris

MADE A FLANK MOVEMENT,

going through the bar-room and out the stable-yard on Shipley street. He thus got a start of half a square on his pursuers, who soon struck the scent and started down Shipley street on a run, getting louder in their talk, having reached a more secluded part of the town. Some of the crowd carried heavy sticks, which they seemed to be ready to use; and such cries as "After him," "Run him out," "Knock him on the head," were the favorites for the time. The crowd was composed of whites and blacks, among the former being members of the Lincoln Republican Club.

HARRIS REINFORCED.

After rattling down Shipley street to a little below Third, Harris had the good fortune to fall in with Sergeant Whelan and Officers Farraday, Bernhardt, Cannon, and Dowling, who formed a body-guard and escorted him calmly to the depot, the crowd following all the way but becoming less demonstrative. The chief object of the mob was to run him out of town, but the temptation to "tap" the fugitive was so strong that had he gone in the direction of the outskirts he would undoubtedly have been injured, perhaps severely.

FOILED! FOILED!

In the language of Dick Deadeye the mob was "foiled" in its attempt, though it did not know it until to-day. It was thought at the time that Harris would leave on the next train, an impression with which he was satisfied; but, after lingering about the defot for some time he slipped away in company with a white friend, and successfully eluded the mob for the night. This morning, however, he came up smiling, and had not yet "shaken the dust of the city from his feet." Harris is not easily bulldozed, whatever else may be said of
john-h-harris-wilmington-1880-08-03.A8:
The Colored Orator.—John H. Harris, the colored orator, of Virginia, who left Bel Air suddenly, weck before last, after gathering some funds for the pretended purpose of publishing a book on the true condition of the negroes in the South, has turned up in Delaware. In attempting to make a Democratic speech to the colored people of New Castle, they commenced to stone him and he was obliged to seek the protection of the Sheriff. He collected about $25 in Wilmington, and says he was prevented by sickness from speaking at Bel Air. This is another case of Ku Kluxing, but as it happens to be on the wrong side it will scarcely be available for Republican campaign matter.

Harris fared even worse in Wilmington, on Tuesday night, than he did at New Castle. He spoke in the city hall, amidst many interruptions from the colored portion of his audience, and when he came out he was pursued and caught by a crowd of colored men. Harris broke loose and escaped, and was finally protected by the police, who escorted him to the depot, where he took the first train—shaking the dust of the city from his feet.
john-h-harris-wilmington-1880-08-03.A13:
How proud a Tennesseean should be to vote for Wright, who stands flat footed in favor of paying the State debt!

We feel an intense interest in the pending Tennessee election. Oh that we could pursue every Tennessee Democrat to vote for John V. Wright for Governor.

INDIANA is hot, hotter, hottest. From one hundred to three hundred Democratic speeches are being made in that State daily from now until the October election. The Democrats count on 20,000 majority.

The nomination of Hancock meets with increased favor every day. Large numbers of Republicans in all parts of the country will cast their votes for him. He will be supported by a large number of this class in New York.

EVERY Kentucky Democrat on the border should put in a good word for John V. Wright, the champion of the National Democracy in Tennessee. His defeat will be a staggering blow to the Democracy in every State in the Union.

JNO. HARRIS, a colored Democratic orator at Wilmington, Del., was chased around town by a mob of black and white Republicans, who were infuriated at a speech be made in defense of Hancock and English. A possee of police took him in charge and protected him from violence.

The news that comes from the canvass in the Northern States is more and more encouraging. The Democrats are everywhere at work with that confidence and enthusiasm that means success. Indiana and New York are certainly ours, and some hope for Ohio, Pennsylvania and Illinois.

Ed. Crossland, Judge-elect of the First District Court, is the ugliest judicial officer in the State, but is smart enough to make up for it.—[Louisville Commercial.

This is a slander upon a passably good looking gentleman. Crossland is a universal favorite with the ladies, and this should be considered a refutation of the above charge. Some "beefy" mortals think no one under a 200 pounder can be "good looking," but by sympathy we indignantly repel the idea of men being judged like cattle.

GENERAL WALKER, Superintendent of the Census, announces that the enumerators will receive their pay within the next thirty days. Receipts will be forwarded to each enumerator, who must sign and forward the receipt, and then he will receive his money. Most people object to receipting for money before they receive it, which is generally a safe rule. But in as much as this is the universal rule of the government, the enumerators must follow it out, and they entertain no fear of losing their money.

There can not be the slighest doubt that the Republicans are pouring negro voters into Ohio and Indiana in the hope of carrying the elections in those States by fraud. The Courier Journal yesterday received from South Union Kentucky, the following information. It comes from one of the best men in the State, a man who is personally known to the publishers of the Courier-Journal: "Nearly all our hired darkies have gone to Indiana and Ohio to vote. Where they get traveling funds from I know not, as most of them lived up close with their wages." It is certainly a bad case with the Republicans when they can not trust their cause to a fair election in Ohio, a conceded Republican State. —Courier Journal.

pink-pratt-marietta-1880-08-24.A1:
A Negro Outrages a White Girl.
Mr. Brit Watkins' eleven year old daughter started to school last Tuesday morning and just as she had entered a small scope of woods, a negro man named, Pink Pratt, laid violent hands upon her, choked her insensible and dragged her from the road to the bushes and raped her person. She was horribly choked, and when she came to her senses, her tongue was protruding from her mouth. She commenced crying and said she was going to tell her father. He pulled out his knife and said he would kill her if she did. She begged him not to kill her and she wouldn't tell. She managed to get home and informed her parents. Constable W. H. White, with a warrant, arrested him with some difficulty. The negro, without being told of the cause of his arrest, said "I will go with you to Mr. Watkins' or anywhere." The uncle of the girl came up and was about to shoot the negro, when Mr. White caught the aimed gun and got it away from him. The negro was tied and brought to Marietta and placed in jail to keep him from being lynched. He waived trial Wednesday morning and is still in durance vile. The girl fully identified him. Mr. Watkins lives seven miles north of Marietta and the negro was working on the same farm for Mr. Charlie Northcutt. We learn this is the third girl he has tried to outrage.

pink-pratt-marietta-1880-08-24.A3:
Barbecues will not be indulged in this campaign and the hungry voter must eat his own sheep meat.

If the gubernatorial canvass should last much longer, some few persons would go crazy for the want of sleep.

Gen. Hansell and D. W. Orr have been nominated for the Legislature. Both good men.

Don't mix too much politics with your profession, it creates prejudice and won't pay.

Mr. J. W. Reid of this county has bought the Hiram Wofford place of 100 acres, paying $1500 for the same.

Another negro man was placed in jail last Friday for an attempt to rape a white lady in this county. Four negroes are in jail now for that offense. This thing must stop.

Good work at lowest prices—Reynolds.

Mass Meeting and Barbecue at Ellijay on Wednesday the 15th of September, when Hon. Thomas M. Notwood and Gen. W.T. Wofford will address the people.

In another column Mr. Geo. L. Daniell is presented as a candidate for Tax Receiver subject to democratic nomination. He has a strong backing, is a worthy man, and would make an efficient officer.

A Dime Club at the residence of Mr. Jas. S. Morris on Thursday evening Sept. 9th, for the benefit of "our little church." All who come can safely anticipate a charming time.

A cat sucking a dog, is one of those stiange occurrences among animals that is hardly creditable, yet such is the fact. Andrew Rogers, the barber, is the owner of the affectionate couple.

Married. By Rev. Walter Manning at Hansell's Factory, on the 5, W. W. Sherman and N. A. Moon, and J. A. Moon to H. L. Braswell, at the house of Mr. Frizby, all of Cobb county.

If you want any kind of Job Printing done, such as Letter Heads, Note Heads, Bill Heads, Cards, Circulars, Handbills, Pamphlets, Tax Receipts, &c., we will guarantee to do the work as cheap as Atlanta. Bring your work to the Journal Office.

Married. On September the 3d, at 3 o'clock p. m., in Omaha City, Nebraska, at the residence of the bride's brother, by the Rev. Maxwell, Mr. Harry 'Sullman, of Marietta, Ga., to Miss Georgia Gaylord of Omaha City. We wish them abundant happiness and prosperity.

We have had lively times in Marietta this week, and enough politics, if it were whisky, to make every man in the county drunk. Monday night, Dr. West, colored, spoke in the court house in behalf of Colquitt, while a colored delegation of four from Atlanta, namely Treadwell, Fannin, Jones and Goodwin, spoke in behalf of Norwood. It was a noisy scene and one we hope never to see again. On Tuesday, the court house was crowded to hear political speeches from Hon. Milton A. Candler, for Norwood, and from Hon. Tom Howard, for Colquitt. Both gentlemen made able and interesting speeches and much enthusiasm prevailed on each side. The crowd was about equally divided for the gubernatorial candidates. It is a hard matter to tell who Cobb county will go for, but---wait and see, age ain't nowhere.

...The Democratic nominating convention of Cobb met in the court house last Tuesday pursuant to a call of the Executive Committee, with a pretty full delegation, Marietta and two other districts, we learn, not being represented. Daniel R. Turner was selected as chairman, and Dr. J. F. Cotton, secretary. It was decided to postpone the nomination of county officers until the first Tuesday in November, in order that all districts may be represented. The convention then went in to the nomination of two members for the lower house of the Legislature. Each delegation present had its candidate and when the call was made things were made lively for awhile. D. W. Orr of Acworth, A. C. McIntosh of Powder Springs, J. H. Ruff of Smyrna, E. Faw and A. J. Hansell of Roswell, J. V. Stanback of Lemons, C. H. Anderson of Powder Springs, and S. B. Love of Smyrna, were presented to the convention. It having been decided to elect by a majority vote, it soon became apparent that names must be dropped. Mr. Jas. H. Ruff, being present, withdrew, and the names of Messrs Love, Stanback, McEachern and others withdrawn by their respective friends. Mr. D. W. Orr, of Acworth, and General A. J. Hansell, of Roswell, were nominated. The convention adjourned to reassemble on the first Tuesday in November to nominate county officers. Messrs. Hansell and Orr have accepted the nomination and will make the race. They are worthy and esteemed citizens and will make faithful representatives.
